newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Macmahon sees A$420 mln turnover.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Macmahon sees A$420 mln turnover.

text.p: Contract mining and civil engineering group Macmahon Holdings Ltd is forecasting a rise in turnover for 1996/97 to more than A$420 million, from last year's A$356.8 million, the company said in its annual report.
Chairman David Munt said nearly 80 percent of this revenue base was already in hand.
In a recent prospectus for a converting preference share issue, Macmahon forecast that pre-tax operating profit for 1996/97 would rise to A$23.8 million from A$15.74 million.
Managing director Graeme Beissel said the underground mining sector offered substantial growth opportunities.

Subject to current negotiations, the National Mine Management underground mining subsidiary, which contributed A$77.5 million in revenue in 1995/96, was expected to see its profile emerge strongly in the eastern Australian states.
"This accelerated presence ... will be achieved through negotiated or tendered entry or by way of acquisition of one of its competitors," the annual report said.
In surface mining, the company would target an expanded involvement in the iron ore sector over the next two years, and in the coal industry over the next three to five years, it said.
The provision of raw materials (rock and sand) to the South East Asian construction industry presented the most favourable opportunities for Macmahon's growth there, it said.
The group's international activities accounted for A$11 million of total turnover in 1995/96 and this was expected to grow substantially during 1996/97, the report said.

The company said the contract mining industry in Australia generally and for Macmahon's selected overseas sectors had strong growth prospects but some pressure could be expected to be exerted from emerging competition in the industry.
Beissel said this might see some rationalisation among all levels of service providers, and Macmahon was well positioned to take advantage of any such changes.
The substantial upfront capital costs for mining projects had resulted in increasing demand on contractors to share the financial risk of a project with the owner, the report said.
